implementation_notes: Kotlin has no using statement, so the stdlib supplies the release scope: the inline extension kotlin.io.use on java.io.Closeable executes the block on the receiver and closes it in a finally, adding a close exception as suppressed when the block also throws. The classic structure - a class that implements close() and releases what it owns, callers invoking it at every exit - is exactly what use calls, so ownership and idempotence stay manual: an owner implements Closeable (or java.lang.AutoCloseable with Kotlin's use overloads) and cascades to its own fields, while call sites write resource.use { }. On targets where no Closeable type exists, a small custom inline use-style function around try/finally is the fallback, and when close must report errors that matter, call close() explicitly as well.
pitfalls: use rethrows the block failure and attaches the close failure as suppressed; code that inspects only the primary exception loses the release error.
use is an extension: a nullable receiver fails to compile in the chain, so write resource?.use { } or handle null explicitly.
Coroutine-era resources (channels, scopes) are not Closeable; they need close/cancel plus invokeOnCompletion, not use.
